profile.idealCustomer: Individuals and families, employers hiring foreign workers, international students, foreign nationals

categories.name: Employers & HR departments hiring foreign talent
categories.opportunity: Employers hiring or retaining foreign nationals need work permits, labour-market assessments, permit extensions, and permanent-residence support for key staff.
categories.rationale: One employer relationship can produce many matters over several years, and the employer often pays. Matters recur as permits expire.

triggers.event: An offer is extended to a candidate who needs a work permit
triggers.whyNeed: Authorisation and timing must be secured before the start date
triggers.whoRecognizes: HR manager or talent acquisition lead
triggers.referralMoment: As soon as the hiring decision is made, before the offer date is fixed
triggers.partnerValue: Avoids failed hires and start-date slippage

triggers.event: A valued employee's work permit or post-graduation permit approaches expiry
triggers.whyNeed: Without a new authorisation or a PR pathway, the employee must stop working
triggers.partnerValue: Retains staff they have already trained

categories.mutualValue: HR teams gain predictable timelines and compliance confidence; you gain recurring corporate matters.
categories.approach: Offer a short briefing for HR teams on permit timelines and employer compliance obligations. Follow up with a simple intake checklist they can use whenever they hire internationally.
digitalAuthority: Publish an employer-focused guide to hiring international graduates and pitch it to HR association newsletters.

categories.name: International recruitment & staffing agencies
categories.opportunity: Recruiters who place foreign candidates encounter immigration questions before the employer or candidate has engaged counsel.
categories.rationale: Recruiters see demand early and in volume, but placements fail if immigration steps are mishandled.

triggers.event: A recruiter shortlists a candidate living abroad
triggers.whyNeed: The candidate needs a work authorisation pathway that fits the role
triggers.partnerValue: Fewer failed placements and faster fee collection

categories.mutualValue: Recruiters protect their placement fees; you gain matters from employers and candidates.
categories.approach: Work only with recruiters who are properly licensed where required. In Ontario, recruiters of foreign nationals must hold a licence. Offer recruiters a quick eligibility pre-screen process they can explain to clients.
categories.decisionMaker: Recruitment agency owner or account manager
categories.regulatoryNote: Recruiters must not charge prohibited fees to foreign workers. Avoid any arrangement where you pay for referrals. Lawyers' referral relationships are regulated. Most jurisdictions prohibit paying or receiving anything of value from non-lawyers for referrals. Where licensee-to-licensee referral fees are allowed, they come with conditions such as client disclosure and fee limits. Build these relationships on reciprocity and expertise. Verify against your law society or bar's current rules.

categories.name: Criminal defence lawyers
categories.opportunity: When a non-citizen is charged, plea and sentencing decisions can have severe immigration consequences. Defence counsel need immigration advice before resolving the case.
categories.rationale: This is a high-stakes, time-sensitive intersection. In Canada, for example, a sentence of six months or more can remove a permanent resident's right to appeal removal. Defence lawyers who understand this need an immigration lawyer they can call quickly.

triggers.event: A non-citizen client is charged with an offence
triggers.whyNeed: The outcome may trigger inadmissibility or removal
triggers.referralMoment: Before any plea or joint sentencing submission
triggers.partnerValue: Protects the client and reduces risk of a later plea challenge

triggers.event: You learn an immigration client has pending charges
triggers.whyNeed: The criminal matter must be handled with immigration consequences in mind
triggers.partnerValue: A well-briefed criminal referral

categories.mutualValue: Defence counsel get fast, specific immigration advice; you get urgent, high-value matters. Referrals flow both ways.
categories.approach: Offer a concise CPD-style session for defence lawyers on immigration consequences of pleas, and a fast consultation line for urgent questions.

categories.name: Licensed immigration consultants (RCICs)
categories.opportunity: Consultants handle applications but cannot represent clients in Federal Court. Refusals that need judicial review, complex inadmissibility, and litigation are natural handoffs to a lawyer.
categories.rationale: Consultants see many refusals first, and judicial review deadlines are short (often 15 days for decisions made in Canada). That creates urgent, well-defined referrals.

triggers.event: A client's application is refused
triggers.whyNeed: Judicial review may be the only remedy, and the filing deadline is short
triggers.partnerValue: They keep the client relationship while the litigation is handled

categories.mutualValue: Consultants can offer clients a litigation pathway without losing them; you gain urgent litigation matters. You can refer straightforward application work back.
categories.approach: Agree in writing how clients move between practices and back. Partner only with consultants in good standing with the regulator.
categories.regulatoryNote: Consultants are regulated by the College of Immigration and Citizenship Consultants. Lawyers' referral relationships are regulated. Most jurisdictions prohibit paying or receiving anything of value from non-lawyers for referrals. assumptions: Immigration clients usually reach a lawyer through someone they already trust: an employer, school, community organisation, or another professional handling a related matter.
Many high-value matters (inadmissibility, refusals, removals) are time-sensitive. Partners who can spot the issue early are more valuable than partners with large audiences.
No typical project value was provided, so commercial-value ratings are relative to the industry, not your own pricing.

guardrails.title: Referral compensation
guardrails.body: Lawyers' referral relationships are regulated. Most jurisdictions prohibit paying or receiving anything of value from non-lawyers for referrals. Where licensee-to-licensee referral fees are allowed, they come with conditions such as client disclosure and fee limits. Build these relationships on reciprocity and expertise. Verify against your law society or bar's current rules.

guardrails.title: Only partner with authorised representatives
guardrails.body: In Canada, only lawyers, Québec notaries, paralegals (in limited contexts), and licensed consultants (RCICs) may represent or advise on immigration matters for a fee. Avoid informal 'agents' or unlicensed intermediaries, because referring to or accepting work through them creates real risk for clients and for you.

guardrails.title: Partnerships are not paid-referral arrangements
guardrails.body: This analysis recommends building relationships based on mutual value. It does not assume that referral fees, commissions, exclusivity, or endorsements are permitted in your industry. Check professional, regulatory, and contractual rules before compensating anyone for referrals.

guardrails.title: Outreach in Canada: CASL applies
guardrails.body: Commercial electronic messages generally need express or implied consent, sender identification, and a working unsubscribe mechanism. Implied consent can exist when a business email address is conspicuously published, the message relates to the recipient's role, and they have not said they don't want such messages. Keep records of how consent was obtained. Personal information you collect is also subject to privacy law (e.g. PIPEDA).

guardrails.title: No automated outreach
guardrails.body: This tool does not contact anyone on your behalf. Every introduction should be personal, relevant to the recipient, and easy to decline.
